notes.21:19: The "burning" refers to the customary royal funeral fire of aromatic spices made in honor of deceased kings of Judah (compare 2 Chronicles 16:14).
notes.22:2: The Masoretic Text reads "forty-two years old," whereas the parallel in 2 Kings 8:26 and some ancient versions read "twenty-two years old" (his father Jehoram died at forty, 21:20). "Daughter of Omri" here denotes granddaughter.
notes.22:6: The Masoretic Text reads "Azariah" here rather than "Ahaziah," an alternate or assimilated form of the king's name (compare 22:1, 7).
notes.22:10: The Masoretic Text employs a rare Hebrew verb meaning "subdued" or "destroyed," corresponding to "destroyed" in the parallel passage at 2 Kings 11:1.
notes.23:11: The Hebrew word for 'testimony' refers to a copy of the covenant law placed in the king's custody at his coronation, echoing Deuteronomy 17:18-19.
notes.23:13: The Hebrew phrase rendered 'those who led the praise' literally means 'those making known to praise,' describing musical directors who guided the liturgical singing.
notes.23:18: The Hebrew literally reads 'the priests, the Levites,' denoting the Levitical priesthood, and 'by the hands of David,' meaning according to David's established order.
notes.24:13: The Hebrew idiom rendered 'the work of restoration went forward' literally says 'healing went up to the work,' picturing the repaired temple as restored to wholeness.
notes.24:20: The Hebrew verb 'clothed' vividly portrays the Spirit of God enveloping and empowering Zechariah for his prophetic proclamation.
notes.24:25: The Masoretic Hebrew reads the plural 'sons of Jehoiada,' while some ancient versions harmonize to the singular in light of verse 20; the plural may indicate additional casualties among Jehoiada's family or serve as a generalizing plural.
notes.24:27: Translated from the qere reading yerev, meaning 'was great' or 'multiplied'; the ketiv reads werov, meaning 'and the greatness' or 'multitude of.' The Hebrew term massa may signify either a prophetic oracle against Joash or a heavy burden laid upon him.
notes.25:8: The Hebrew opening is terse and ironic, conceding Amaziah's determination to march with the northern mercenaries while warning that God will still cause him to stumble before the enemy.
notes.25:16: The Hebrew text weaves a sharp wordplay on the root for counsel across the king's rebuke ("counselor"), the prophet's warning ("determined," literally "counseled," and "my counsel"), and the king's next move in verse seventeen ("took counsel").
notes.25:23: The Hebrew text reads "Jehoahaz," an inverted form of the name Ahaziah used for Amaziah's grandfather (cf. 21:17); "Corner Gate" literally translates "the Turning Gate."
notes.25:28: The Masoretic text literally reads "the City of Judah," referring to Jerusalem as the capital city of Judah.
notes.26:3: Translates the qere reading "Jecoliah" (Yekolyah); the ketiv spells the name with an extra yod (Yekilyah).
notes.26:5: The Masoretic text literally reads "in the visions of God" (from the verb "to see"), describing Zechariah's prophetic discernment.
notes.26:7: Translates the qere form for "the Arabians" (ha-Arvim); the ketiv preserves a longer gentilic spelling (ha-Arviyyim) with the same meaning.
notes.26:11: Translates the qere reading "Jeiel" (Yeiel); the ketiv reads "Jeuel" (Yeuel).
notes.26:21: Translates the qere reading "a separate house" (bet ha-chofshit), denoting a secluded residence for a leper; the ketiv reads an abstract plural form (ha-chofshut) with the same sense.
notes.27:3: Ophel was the fortified southern spur of Jerusalem lying between the temple mount and the City of David.
notes.27:5: A kor was a large Hebrew dry measure equal to ten ephahs (roughly six bushels, or about two hundred twenty liters).
notes.28:3: The Masoretic Hebrew verb here explicitly means burned, whereas the parallel account in Second Kings sixteen verse three uses a verb meaning caused to pass through.
notes.28:16: The Masoretic Text reads the plural, kings of Assyria, likely referring to the Assyrian royal line or imperial administration.
notes.28:19: Chronicles here refers to Ahaz as king of Israel, using Israel as a covenantal title for the kingdom of Judah.
notes.28:20: Chronicles consistently renders the Assyrian monarch's name as Tilgath-Pilneser rather than Tiglath-Pileser.
notes.29:8: The Hebrew qere reads lezaavah, meaning an object of terror or trembling, while the ketiv reverses the middle letters with the same sense.
notes.29:13: Following the Hebrew qere, the name reads Jeiel; the ketiv reads Jeuel.
notes.29:14: Following the Hebrew qere, the name reads Jehiel; the ketiv reads Jehuel.
notes.29:28: Following the Hebrew qere, the participle reads machtserim, sounded the trumpets; the ketiv preserves the longer spelling mechatstserim.
notes.30:5: The Hebrew phrase literally means "in great numbers" or "in multitude," referring to nationwide observance, though some understand it temporally as "for a long time."
notes.30:8: "Yield your hand" renders a Hebrew idiom meaning literally "give a hand," denoting submission and pledged allegiance.
notes.30:18: The Masoretic verse division separates the preposition "for" at the close of verse eighteen from its object at the opening of verse nineteen, carrying Hezekiah's prayer across both verses.
notes.30:27: The Hebrew places "the priests" and "the Levites" in direct apposition without a conjunction, expressing the traditional designation "the Levitical priests."
notes.31:2: "The camps of the LORD" translates a plural Hebrew noun portraying the temple precincts and courts in imagery drawn from Israel's wilderness encampment.
notes.31:12: The ketiv (written text) spells the Levite's name with an extra vowel letter, while the qere (read form) followed here reads Conaniah; the same spelling variation occurs in verse thirteen.
notes.31:16: The terse administrative wording of verses sixteen through eighteen outlines how distributions in the priestly cities operated alongside the genealogical registers for those ministering at the temple.
notes.32:21: The Masoretic Qere reads plural construct 'and some of those who came forth from his own body' (rendered 'some of his own offspring'), whereas the Ketiv has a singular form.
notes.32:22: The Masoretic Hebrew reads 'and guided them on every side,' whereas the Septuagint and Vulgate read 'and gave them rest.'
notes.32:28: The Masoretic Hebrew literally reads 'and flocks for the folds,' reversing the expected order 'folds for the flocks.'
notes.33:11: The Hebrew 'with hooks' reflects the Assyrian practice of leading captives with hooks or rings, though the same noun can also mean 'thorns.'
notes.33:16: The Masoretic Qere reads 'rebuilt' (or 'built'), which is followed here; the Ketiv reads 'prepared' (or 'restored').
notes.33:19: The Masoretic Text reads 'Hozai' as a proper name, though the form closely resembles the plural noun 'seers' used in verse eighteen.
notes.34:5: The qere reads "upon their altars," while the ketiv preserves an alternative plural suffix spelling with the same sense.
notes.34:6: The qere reads "in their ruined places" (also understood by some traditional interpreters as "with their axes" or "with their mattocks"), whereas the ketiv divides the consonants into two words meaning "he searched their houses."
notes.34:9: The qere reads "and they returned to Jerusalem," while the ketiv reads "and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem."
notes.34:22: The qere gives the spelling Tokhath (ketiv reads a fuller vowel spelling of the same name), called Tikvah in 2 Kings 22:14. The Second Quarter refers to the newer western expansion of Jerusalem.
notes.35:3: The qere reads the active participle "who taught" (or "who instructed"), while the ketiv reflects a variant orthographic form of the same verb.
notes.35:4: The qere reads the Hiphil imperative "prepare yourselves" (or "make preparation"), whereas the ketiv reads the Niphal imperative "be prepared."
notes.35:25: The "Laments" mentioned here are a collection of national elegies mourning King Josiah, distinct from the biblical Book of Lamentations, which mourns the later destruction of Jerusalem.
notes.36:9: The Masoretic Text reads eight years here, whereas the parallel account in 2 Kings 24:8 states that Jehoiachin was eighteen years old.
notes.36:10: The Hebrew term for brother is used here in the wider sense of kinsman, since Zedekiah was Jehoiachin's uncle.
notes.36:14: The Masoretic qere reads the defective infinitive construct paired with its cognate noun to intensify the charge of covenant unfaithfulness, whereas the ketiv records a fuller orthographic spelling.
notes.36:17: The Masoretic qere reads the standard plural gentilic for Chaldeans, while the ketiv preserves an alternative longer spelling.
